edges.rationale: Error detection/correction is one of the link-layer services introduced here; understanding where these techniques operate requires the framing/encapsulation model and the notion of link-layer services.
Multiple access protocols coordinate access to a shared broadcast channel, a concept defined in the introduction's coverage of broadcast vs. point-to-point links.
Understanding why broadcast channels need node-level addressing and how frames carry addresses builds on the framing and broadcast-link concepts from the introduction.
Ethernet framing and link-access presuppose the general framing/encapsulation and link-access services described in the introduction.
MPLS is framed as providing link-layer services between IP routers, which only makes sense once the link layer's service model is understood.
Ethernet frames carry a CRC field and adapters use CRC to detect frame errors, so the CRC technique should be learned before studying Ethernet framing and frame processing.
Classic shared-media Ethernet is built on CSMA/CD, a random-access protocol covered in Multiple Access Protocols; understanding Ethernet's medium access requires that background.
Switch forwarding/filtering and self-learning operate on MAC addresses, and frame delivery between hosts relies on ARP-resolved MAC addresses, so addressing must precede switches.
VLANs are created by configuring link-layer switches (traffic isolation, trunking over switch infrastructure); they cannot be understood without the switch model.
MPLS label switching is best understood in contrast to link-layer switching vs. IP routing, and data center designs are built on switched topologies covered in the switches topic.
